name: Yumi Bow
powers: Exceptional range and accuracy; used in court archery contests.
description: The yumi is a tall asymmetrical bow used by samurai and nobles. Its distinctive shape allowed for powerful shots and was a status symbol in Heian-era archery tournaments.

name: Yata no Kagami
powers: Reflects truth and brilliance; part of the imperial regalia.
description: The Eight-Fold Mirror hung from a sacred sakaki tree outside the cave where Amaterasu hid, its brilliance luring the sun goddess back to illuminate the world. Revered at Ise Grand Shrine as one of the Three Sacred Treasures, it stands for truth and for the imperial line's legitimacy in Japanese myth.

name: Yasakani no Magatama
powers: Symbolizes benevolent fortune and the sovereign's right to rule.
description: The curved jade bead (magatama) dangled from the branch of the sacred sakaki tree beside the mirror that drew Amaterasu from her cave. Counted among the Three Sacred Treasures of Japan, it symbolizes benevolent fortune and the sovereign's mandate, and its comma shape recurs in tomb jewelry from the Kofun period.

name: Yeouiju
powers: Grants wishes; lets the imugi become a dragon
description: The wish-granting jewel (yeouiju) of Korean lore, the prize that a serpent imugi must grasp to climb into dragonhood. Said to grant any wish to its holder, it appears in tales of serpents waiting years for the jewel to fall from the sky, as in the story of the imugi that lost it at the waterfall.

name: Yeibichai Mask
material: Painted buckskin with feathers and turquoise
powers: Lets a dancer embody a Holy Person in ceremony.
description: The painted buckskin mask worn by Navajo dancers so they may embody the Holy People (ye'i) in the great nightway ceremonies, healing rites whose chants invoke Changing Woman and the blessing of the gods. Made anew for each ceremony and used only by initiated singers, the masks are never sold or displayed, and carry the marks that identify each Holy Person to the community.
source: Navajo oral tradition and ceremonial practice

name: Ade (Yoruba Beaded Crown)
material: Glass beads, velvet or cotton cloth, seed beads
description: The ade is the beaded crown of Yoruba obas, a cone- or basket-shaped headdress whose beaded fringe veils the wearer's face. Its patterns include birds, the Ogboni-eye emblem, and the divine king's face, tying the ruler to Oduduwa and the orisa. Coronation tradition holds the veil protects subjects from the king's overwhelming gaze.
source: Yoruba coronation tradition; museum collections (British Museum, Musée du quai Branly)
